items.stem: What actually leaves the device when a student presses Buy?

options.label: The entire screen, copied to the server
A small structured message with named fields such as ticketId, quantity and requestId
The student's whole browsing history
Nothing; the server watches the screen directly

items.hint_text: The application builds a message; it does not ship the screen.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The application turns the action into a structured message called the payload.
items.feedback_wrong: The screen never travels. The interface builds a structured payload with named fields the server can read, sends it across the network, and later renders whatever response returns.

items.stem: Two students see '1 ticket remaining' and press Buy at the same moment. Who can decide which buyer gets it?

options.label: Whichever browser loaded the page fastest
Each browser decides for its own user
A shared server that receives both requests and reserves the ticket once
Nobody; the ticket goes to both

items.hint_text: Each device knows only part of what is happening.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The shared server owns the truth and reserves the ticket for one request.
items.feedback_wrong: Both browsers only believe the ticket is available; neither sees the other buyer. A shared system must own the truth, reserve the ticket once, and send a different answer to the second request.

items.stem: A user presses Save and the screen instantly shows 'Saved', but the network request actually failed. What happened?

options.label: It was saved anyway, because the screen said so
The interface displayed success before the server confirmed it
The server always confirms a save instantly
The cache deleted the record

items.hint_text: A changed button is not a confirmation.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The screen changing is only the interface reacting; success requires the server's response.
items.feedback_wrong: The interface showed success on its own, before any confirmation arrived. The button changing does not prove the action succeeded, so honest products design a loading state and handle the failure when it comes back.

items.stem: Take the address https://api.stagepass.app/events/441/tickets/9082/reserve. Which parts does it contain? Select all that apply.

options.label: The communication rules, where HTTPS also protects the message in transit
A domain name whose network address is found through DNS
A path naming a specific capability, here reserving ticket 9082
The server's stored price for the ticket

items.hint_text: An address describes how to talk, where to go, and which capability to use.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The URL carries the protocol rules, the domain and the path; the price lives in the server's database.
items.feedback_wrong: A URL holds the communication rules, a domain DNS translates to a network address, and a path naming a capability. Data such as the price is not inside the address; the server reads it from its own storage.

items.stem: An AI image takes thirty seconds to generate. Which conversation pattern fits best?

options.label: Keep one browser request open until the image is finished
Create a job, return a job ID immediately, then poll the status or stream the result
Send the same request twice so it finishes sooner
Store nothing and hope the connection holds

items.hint_text: Long work should not hold a request open forever.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. A job lets the server accept the work instantly and report progress later.
items.feedback_wrong: Long-running work is modelled as a job: the server returns a job ID immediately, does the work in the background, and the application polls the status or streams the result. Holding one request open risks timeouts.

items.stem: A request body reads '9082, 441, 1, 7719' with no field names. Why is that fragile?

options.label: Numbers cannot travel over the internet
Neither system can be sure which value is the ticket, the event, the quantity or the attempt; named fields create agreement
The message is too short to be a request
Servers automatically reject unnamed values

items.hint_text: Structure is what makes a message meaningful.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. Named fields let both systems agree on what each value means.
items.feedback_wrong: Bare values are ambiguous: is 1 a quantity, a ticket or an attempt? Named fields such as ticketId and requestId are the shared agreement that lets the server interpret the message correctly.

items.stem: Which checks belong on the server when it receives a purchase request? Select all that apply.

options.label: Whether the ticket exists and is still available
Whether the user is signed in and allowed to buy it
Whether this exact request has already been processed
Whether the Buy button looked convincing on the screen

items.hint_text: The server trusts its own records, not the screen.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The server validates existence, availability, identity, permission and whether the request was already handled.
items.feedback_wrong: The server must verify the ticket exists and is available, authenticate and authorize the user, and recognize a retried request. How the screen looked is irrelevant; the server reads its own stored truth.

items.stem: Why does a purchase request carry a unique request ID such as purchase-attempt-7719?

options.label: So the server can recognize a retried request and return the existing result instead of charging twice
So the browser loads faster
To encrypt the ticket price
To identify the student's device model

items.hint_text: Think about what happens when nothing seems to happen.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. A repeated request ID is recognized as the same attempt, so the action is never performed twice.
items.feedback_wrong: When a slow request makes a user click again, the server receives a duplicate. A unique request ID lets it spot the retry and return the same result; retrying the same action should not perform it twice.

options.label: The physical location of the server
A specific capability exposed at a particular path, such as /reserve or /messages
The user's own device
The cable carrying the request

items.hint_text: It is not just where the server is, but which ability you are calling.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. An endpoint names a particular capability, and clear paths like /tournaments/88/report-result reveal what a system can do.
items.feedback_wrong: An endpoint is a capability at a path, not a machine or a cable. A vague one like /saveData hides what the system does; a clear one like /events/441/reserve announces the capability.

items.stem: How should a 'Maya is typing...' indicator in a chat app be delivered?

options.label: Stored permanently like a message, so it can be reviewed later
Sent over an ongoing live connection as a temporary event that expires quickly
Pushed by reloading the whole page
Polled by asking the server once per hour

items.hint_text: Nobody needs to retrieve that Maya typed for 1.8 seconds last Tuesday.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. Typing indicators are temporary events on a live connection; messages are what get stored.
items.feedback_wrong: A typing indicator is a temporary live event: sent over an ongoing connection and expired after a short timeout. Messages should be stored permanently; typing events should not.

items.stem: What is the payload of a request?

options.label: The layout of the screen that sent it
The information carried inside the request, such as form answers, filters, identifiers or an image
The server's database
The domain name the request was sent to

items.hint_text: It is the content of the message, not the address.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The payload is the information inside the request.
items.feedback_wrong: The payload is what the request carries: form answers, search filters, an identifier, a file. The domain and path say where it goes; the payload says what it means.

items.stem: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?

options.label: Authentication checks who the user is; authorization checks what that user is allowed to do
They are two names for the same check
Authentication is the password field; authorization is the login button
Authorization checks who the user is; authentication checks permissions

items.hint_text: One reads the name tag; the other reads the permission.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. Authentication is identity; authorization is permission.
items.feedback_wrong: Authentication answers who is this user, and authorization answers may this user do this action. A signed-in student is authenticated but still not authorized to edit another team's score.

items.stem: A signed-in student sends a request to delete another team's score. Which response fits?

options.label: Unauthorized, because the user is not signed in
Forbidden, because the user is identified but not allowed
Empty, because nothing was deleted
Success, because the request was well-formed

items.hint_text: The user passed the name-tag check but failed the permission check.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. Forbidden means authenticated but not authorized.
items.feedback_wrong: The student is signed in, so authentication passed and Unauthorized does not fit. The action is not permitted, which is Forbidden: identified, but not allowed.

items.stem: Which statements about a request-response conversation are true? Select all that apply.

options.label: The request is a structured message sent to another system
The interface decides what to show based on the response
The browser's copy of shared data is always the final truth
A request always succeeds as long as the button works

items.hint_text: Think about who owns the truth and what can fail.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. The request is a structured message, and the interface renders whatever the response describes.
items.feedback_wrong: A request is a structured message and the interface shows what the response reports. The browser is never the final authority on shared data, and a working button does not make a request succeed.

items.stem: An app must load a playlist containing five thousand songs. Which conversation pattern fits best?

options.label: Download all five thousand entries in one response
Load the first page of songs, then request the next page as the user scrolls
Stream every song's audio at once
Create a background job and poll until it finishes

items.hint_text: Retrieving unnecessary information makes the product slower and more expensive.
items.feedback_correct: Correct. Pagination retrieves a large collection in smaller groups on demand.
items.feedback_wrong: Pulling all five thousand at once is slow and wasteful. Pagination loads the first twenty or so and fetches the next group when the user reaches the bottom.
